name: Sprint

profile.address: 600, Sea Girt Avenue, Manasquan, Monmouth County, New Jersey, 08736
profile.reading:
The Manasquan cable landing station on the New Jersey shore was one of the six shore ends of TAT-14, the fourteenth in the historic series of consortium built transatlantic telecommunications cables linking the United States to Europe. TAT-14 entered service on March 21, 2001, built and financed by a consortium of more than thirty telecommunications carriers, among them AT&T, BT Group, Deutsche Telekom, Vodafone, Verizon Communications, Orange, and Telefonica, reflecting the scale of investment required to lay a 15,428 kilometer fiber optic cable system across the North Atlantic.

TAT-14 was engineered as a self healing ring rather than a simple point to point link, with landing points at Manasquan and Tuckerton in New Jersey on the American side, and at Blaabjerg in Denmark, Norden in Germany, Katwijk in the Netherlands, Saint-Valery-en-Caux in France, and Widemouth Bay in the United Kingdom on the European side. That ring topology meant traffic could reroute around a cable break at any single landing point, a design consideration that mattered enormously given how much transatlantic financial and telecommunications traffic these systems carried at the time. The system had a design capacity of 9.38 terabits per second, with 3.15 terabits per second actually lit and in commercial use, figures that made TAT-14 one of the higher capacity transatlantic systems of its generation when it launched.

The cable's operational life ended on December 15, 2020, when the consortium decommissioned it, not long after newer fiber systems with far greater capacity entered service on the same transatlantic route. Dismantling of cable segments began in 2021, with recovered materials sent to environmental services companies for recycling, the standard end of life process for a retired submarine cable system.

This registry lists Sprint as the facility's operator, a designation that predates TAT-14's decommissioning and reflects Sprint's position as one of the consortium's original American landing party members rather than sole ownership of the system, which was always a shared consortium asset spanning dozens of carriers. Cable landing stations of this kind function as the buildings where undersea fiber comes ashore and connects into terrestrial networks, carrier infrastructure rather than commercial colocation space, and they do not publish square footage, power capacity, or tenancy figures the way a commercial data center would. With TAT-14 itself now retired, the building's role since 2021 is not part of the public record.

reading:
Sprint Corporation no longer exists. It merged into T-Mobile US on 1 April 2020, and the building this registry attaches to the Sprint name is a cable landing station in Manasquan, New Jersey, that served a transatlantic cable retired later the same year. The row survives because of a stale name in an assessment roll and a bulk retag in OpenStreetMap, not because Sprint operates a data centre anywhere.

The Manasquan station was one of the shore ends of TAT-14, a consortium cable that entered service in 2001 linking the United States to the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands, engineered as a self healing ring with two American landings, Manasquan and Tuckerton. Sprint was one of the original consortium members alongside AT&T, Verizon, Deutsche Telekom and others, each responsible for a segment of a shared asset rather than owning the system outright. TAT-14 was decommissioned on 15 December 2020, and recovery of cable segments began the following year.

The Monmouth County land records identify the building precisely. Manasquan Borough block 54, lot 1 is a commercial parcel of 20,140 square feet, about 0.462 acres, in the B-3 zone, carrying a two storey masonry building of 19,470 square feet built in 2000, one year before TAT-14 went live. The assessment roll still names the owner as Sprint Communications Company LP, care of a property tax department at a post office box in Bellevue, Washington, which is T-Mobile's corporate home. The deed history is clearer than the owner line. Sprint Communications Company LP took title on 26 June 2014 at a recorded 999,000 dollars, and on 26 April 2023 the parcel was conveyed to T-Mobile Northeast LLC for a recorded 10 dollars, a nominal intra group transfer. The roll's owner name has simply not caught up with the deed. The roll also gives the property location as 50 Camp Drive, not the 600 Sea Girt Avenue carried in the OpenStreetMap address tags, though the two points sit within about sixty metres of one another.

The tag that put this building into a data centre registry is newer than all of that. The outline was imported from Microsoft building footprints in 2023 with no tags of substance. On 11 August 2026, changeset 187297122 named it, attributed it to Sprint and tagged it telecom=exchange, citing a submarine cable reference site. Eight days later, on 19 August 2026, changeset 187694316 retagged it with the comment "Updated underseas Cable Landing Stations to [telecom:Data Center] rather than [telecom:exchange]". That single editorial decision, applied across a set of landing stations, is the entire reason a 19,470 square foot carrier building for a decommissioned cable now sits in a list alongside multi hundred megawatt campuses.

Nothing about power belongs on this page. Cable landing stations do not publish IT load, utility service or standby generation, no such figures exist for this one, and the cable it was built to terminate has been out of service since 2020. The honest reading of this row is a small shore end building, owned since 2023 by T-Mobile Northeast LLC, whose working life as international infrastructure has ended.
